The core reasoning revolves around the duality of rational postulates versus empirical facts. Postulates of rationality—such as causal containment and conservation principles—are foundational to interpreting natural phenomena. These principles are not empirically verifiable per se but are necessary for coherence in scientific description. In GSI, they form the basis of Bayesian inference by defining prior constraints on possible outcomes. In GSE, they govern state transitions through conservation laws and logical consistency. The failure mode occurs when empirical observations contradict these postulates, indicating either a breakdown in the model or emergence of new dynamics. The tension between Darwinian evolution and conservation laws is resolved by distinguishing between accidental and essential changes: if species evolve through modification of existing forms, then change remains within the bounds of conservation; if not, the system risks self-destruction—a contradiction to natural tendency toward stability.
